title: Raman spectroscopy
wiki_lead:
Raman spectroscopy (; named after the physicist C. V. Raman) is a spectroscopic technique typically used to determine vibrational modes of molecules, although rotational and other low-frequency modes of systems may also be observed. Raman spectroscopy is commonly used in chemistry to provide a structural fingerprint by which molecules can be identified.
Raman spectroscopy relies upon inelastic scattering of photons, known as Raman scattering. A source of monochromatic light, usually from a laser in the visible, near infrared, or near ultraviolet range is used, although X-rays can also be used. The laser light interacts with molecular vibrations, phonons or other excitations in the system, resulting in the energy of the laser photons being shifted up or down. The shift in energy gives information about the vibrational modes in the system. Time-resolved spectroscopy and infrared spectroscopy typically yield similar yet complementary information.
Typically, a sample is illuminated with a laser beam. Electromagnetic radiation scattered from the illuminated spot is collected with a lens. Raman scattering is typically very weak. As a result, for many years the main difficulty in collecting Raman spectra was separating the weak inelastically scattered light from the intense Rayleigh scattered laser light (referred to as "laser rejection"). Elastic scattered radiation at the wavelength corresponding to the laser line (Rayleigh scattering) is filtered out by either a notch filter, edge pass filter, or a band pass filter, while the rest of the collected light is dispersed onto a detector.
Spontaneous Raman scattering is typically very weak. Historically, Raman spectrometers used holographic gratings and multiple dispersion stages to achieve a high degree of laser rejection. In the past, photomultipliers were the detectors of choice for dispersive Raman setups, which resulted in long acquisition times. However, modern instrumentation almost universally employs notch or edge filters for laser rejection. Dispersive single-stage spectrographs (axial transmissive (AT) or Czerny–Turner (CT) monochromators) paired with CCD detectors are most common although Fourier transform (FT) spectrometers are also common for use with NIR lasers.
The name "Raman spectroscopy" typically refers to vibrational Raman spectroscopy using laser wavelengths which are not absorbed by the sample. There are many variations of Raman spectroscopy including surface-enhanced Raman, resonance Raman, tip-enhanced Raman, polarized Raman, stimulated Raman, transmission Raman, spatially-offset Raman, and hyper Raman. Raman scattering is not limited to molecular vibration, and it can be applied to rotational, rovibronic, and electronic spectroscopy.

History
Although the inelastic scattering of light was predicted by Adolf Smekal in 1923, it was not observed in practice until 1928. The Raman effect was named after one of its discoverers, the Indian scientist C. V. Raman, who observed the effect
grok_lead: Raman spectroscopy is an analytical technique that utilizes the inelastic scattering of monochromatic light to probe the vibrational, rotational, and other low-frequency modes in molecules, providing detailed information about their chemical structure and composition. This method, based on the Raman effect, enables non-destructive analysis of samples in solid, liquid, or gaseous states, making it invaluable for fields such as chemistry, biology, materials science, and pharmaceuticals. The technique was discovered in 1928 by Indian physicist Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, who observed that a small portion of scattered light from liquids acquires wavelengths different from the incident light, leading to his award of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for this groundbreaking work on light scattering. The fundamental principle of Raman spectroscopy relies on the interaction between incident photons and molecular vibrations: when a molecule absorbs a photon, it may enter a virtual excited state and re-emit a photon of slightly different energy, resulting in a frequency shift (Stokes or anti-Stokes lines) that corresponds to the energy difference of the molecular transition. This inelastic scattering occurs because the polarizability of the molecule changes during vibration, unlike elastic Rayleigh scattering where the frequency remains unchanged. Typically, a laser serves as the excitation source, with the scattered light collected and analyzed using a spectrometer to generate a spectrum where peaks indicate specific molecular bonds or functional groups. The cross-section for Raman scattering is inherently weakâabout 10^{-6} to 10^{-8} times that of fluorescence ânecessitating sensitive detectors and often enhancements like surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) for trace detection. Since its inception, Raman spectroscopy has evolved from basic laboratory setups to advanced variants, including confocal Raman microscopy for spatial mapping at micrometer resolution and time-resolved techniques for studying ultrafast dynamics. Its non-invasive nature allows in vivo applications, such as diagnosing diseases through tissue analysis or monitoring biopharmaceutical processes in real-time. Key advantages include minimal sample preparation, high specificity for molecular fingerprints, and compatibility with aqueous environments, which is particularly useful in biological studies where water's Raman signal is less interfering than in infrared spectroscopy. Today, it remains a cornerstone tool in scientific research and industrial quality control, continually advancing with innovations in laser technology and computational analysis.
